front: Fairness and bias: which one is the goal and which one is the problem?
back: Fairness is the goal: results that don't create unjustified differences between groups. Bias is the problem that stands in its way, usually coming from the data or from how the problem was set up.

front: What does robustness mean in responsible AI?
back: Giving dependable results even when inputs are unusual, noisy or deliberately adversarial. For example, Trailmate should still answer sensibly when a customer misspells every word.

front: Which responsible AI feature does a hallucination breach?
back: Veracity, meaning truthfulness. A model that confidently states invented facts, such as a made-up refund policy, has a veracity problem.

front: Explainability vs. transparency: how do they differ?
back: Explainability is understanding why a model produced a result. Transparency is being open with users and stakeholders that AI is involved and how it works.

front: Cairnway's chatbot must never discuss medical advice for injuries. Which Guardrails safeguard fits?
back: A denied topic. You define off-limit topics, and the guardrail helps block them in both questions and answers. Content filters cover harmful categories such as hate or violence instead.

front: Which Guardrails feature flags answers not supported by the source documents in a RAG app?
back: Contextual grounding checks. They score each answer for grounding (supported by the source) and relevance (answers the question). Answers below your threshold are treated as hallucinations.

front: Guardrails or Bedrock Model Evaluation: which one tests a model before you choose it?
back: Model Evaluation. It scores accuracy, robustness and toxicity on built-in or your own datasets. Guardrails instead act at runtime, checking what goes into and comes out of the model.

front: Why is the smallest model that meets the need the more responsible choice?
back: Training and running large models uses a lot of electricity. A right-sized model gives the needed quality with lower cost, speed and energy use, and so lower carbon emissions.

front: Name two ways to cut a model's environmental impact besides picking a smaller one.
back: Reuse an existing model instead of training a new one, and avoid unnecessary retraining. Choosing a Region that uses cleaner energy can also matter.

front: Cairnway's review sentiment task passes evaluation with a small model. Why not pick the largest anyway?
back: The small model meets the requirement and is cheaper, faster and uses less energy. Responsible selection means choosing by need and risk, not by size.

front: List the five generative AI legal and business risks the exam guide names.
back: Intellectual property infringement claims, biased model outputs, loss of customer trust, end user risk and hallucinations.

front: How can a hallucination become a legal risk for Cairnway?
back: A company can be held to what its chatbot promises. If Trailmate invents a 90-day return window when the real policy says 30, Cairnway may face a dispute.

front: Why are biased outputs especially risky in hiring, lending and insurance?
back: They can break anti-discrimination law. A model that learned from unfair past decisions may treat equally good candidates or applicants differently by group.

front: Why does a balanced dataset matter?
back: If one group or outcome dominates, such as 95% of examples from one group, the model learns that group best and serves the others worse.

front: Why is an English-only support dataset a problem for Cairnway's German customers?
back: The data is not inclusive or diverse. A model learns from the people, languages and situations it saw, so it will serve missing groups badly.

front: Why check label quality in a supervised dataset?
back: Humans attach the labels, such as fraud or not fraud. If labellers are careless or biased, the model learns their mistakes. Several reviewers should agree and avoid stereotypes.

front: A model scores very well on training data but poorly on new data. What is the problem?
back: Overfitting, also called high variance. The model memorized details and coincidences in the training data instead of the real patterns.

front: A model performs poorly on both training and test data. What is the problem?
back: Underfitting, also called high bias. The model is too simple or rests on wrong assumptions, so it misses real patterns.

front: How can an overall accurate model still harm a demographic group?
back: Overall accuracy can hide poor accuracy for one group, for example when training data under-represents them. That is why you test accuracy by group, not just overall.

front: What is the bias-variance trade-off?
back: Making a model more complex lowers bias but raises variance, and the reverse. The goal is a balance that captures real patterns without memorizing noise.

front: What is subgroup analysis and what does it reveal?
back: You measure accuracy and error rates separately for each group, such as by age band or region, and compare them. A big gap is a fairness warning that overall accuracy hides.

front: Name three human or process methods to check a system for bias and truthfulness.
back: Analyzing label quality, subgroup analysis and human audits, including deliberately testing with tricky or hostile prompts, sometimes called red teaming.

front: Why must a responsible team keep monitoring a model after launch?
back: Models drift as the real world changes, and bias can creep in. Comparing production behaviour with a baseline, plus user feedback and complaints, gives early warning.

front: Which tool fits each stage: model choice, data bias, bias drift, human review, runtime safety?
back: Bedrock Model Evaluation for model choice, SageMaker Clarify for data bias, Model Monitor for bias drift, Amazon A2I for human review and Bedrock Guardrails for runtime safety.
